posts.text:
This looks like a map of cars. It's almost the opposite. The palest countries are the ones with the most vehicles per person — road deaths peak almost exactly where car ownership is lowest.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

a thread 🧵🗺️
1/ The regional gap first. The WHO puts road deaths at about 19 per 100,000 people across Africa and under 7 across Europe. Same measure, same year, nearly a threefold difference.
2/ And it isn't about traffic volume. Low-income countries hold roughly 1% of the world's registered cars and account for about 16% of the world's road deaths.
3/ Zimbabwe is the darkest country in Africa on these figures, above 40 per 100,000. Liberia, Eritrea, South Sudan, Namibia, Malawi and the DR Congo all sit in the 30s.

4/ Why: older vehicles, no separated footways, roads where pedestrians and freight travel at the same speed in the same lane, and trauma care measured in hours rather than minutes. Surviving the crash is half the story.

5/ South-East Asia's dark band is a different mechanism — Vietnam above 30, Thailand around 25. These are motorcycle countries, and a motorcycle puts no structure at all between the rider and the road.

6/ The pale countries track wealth closely, with one loud exception. The US sits near 14 per 100,000 against 3.3 for Germany, 2.6 for the UK and 2.1 for Japan, Norway and Sweden. Rich is not automatically safe.

7/ One caveat about the map itself. These are 2019 modelled estimates and they move: the Dominican Republic showed above 60 per 100,000 in that round and appears nearer 28 in more recent national reporting.

8/ The pattern underneath holds. Around 1.2 to 1.3 million deaths a year, roughly 77% of them male, with adults aged 15 to 44 accounting for about 59% of the total.

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)
